sections.report:
**Walk (working notes, The whole piece)**

First read: the eye lands on the bold headline "Notes for ferry passengers" at the top left, then drops into three paragraphs whose lines are jammed together and overlap, so reading slows right away. It looks like a plain informational page for ferry riders. It feels neutral and utilitarian, but broken. Assumed job: tell ferry passengers about the schedule, bicycles, and winter timetable on a web page or notice. Image is about 1280×800, about one screen, so no crops. (Bash was refused, so I didn't run crop.mjs or entries.mjs and worked from the whole image.)

- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for? **yes**. The headline says it.
- Do the main image and the headline make one idea together? **yes**. There is no main image, so this doesn't apply.
- Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job? **yes**. There is only a heading and three paragraphs, with no ornament.
- Apart from the pictures, do the type, colors, and shapes share one mood and era? **yes**. It uses one sans family in dark grey on white.
- Is the copy finished, with no placeholder text and no spelling mistakes? **yes**. I read all three paragraphs and found no typos or placeholder text.
- Within one screen, does each kind of element look the same everywhere? **yes**. All three paragraphs share the same style.
- Do the colors, shapes, and directions carry the mood the message calls for? **yes**. A calm, neutral look suits a practical notice.
- Does each heading name what its section holds? **yes**. "Notes for ferry passengers" covers the content.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so I skipped step 5.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

(Outside my section, for the director: the lines in all three paragraphs overlap. In the first paragraph (x 120–750, y 137–200), the baselines are about 15 px apart on type that looks about 18 px, so ascenders and descenders collide ("forty minutes…" runs into "takes about…"). The same happens at y 216–280 and y 296–360. This is the defect that decides whether this page works, and it belongs under Text, at the line about space between lines. Arrangement should also look at the empty right 40% and lower half of the page.)

**What's working.**
- The headline "Notes for ferry passengers" (x 120–567, y 75–110) is the only bold, large element. It tells a stranger what the page is and who it's for at a glance.
- The copy is complete and concrete. It gives real details a passenger acts on: every forty minutes, about twelve minutes, bicycles free on the lower deck, one boat an hour in winter, the last crossing before dusk. Each paragraph covers one topic.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk: What matters first** (Bash is unavailable here, so I couldn't run the crop script. At about 1280×800 the image is one screen, so I worked from the whole image.)

First read: the eye lands on the bold headline "Notes for ferry passengers" (x≈120–567, y≈75–110), then drops into three paragraphs. The lines in those paragraphs overlap each other and are hard to read. It looks like a passenger notice for a river ferry, plain and informational. Assumed job: a notice that passengers scan for schedule, bicycle and winter rules.

- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? **Yes.** The headline is about twice the body size and bold.
- Can you tell each level of text from the next at a glance? **Yes.** There are only two levels, title and body, and the gap between them is large.
- Where headings are larger, do they also differ in weight, form or color? **Yes.** The headline is bold and the body is regular.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headline clearly leads.** "Notes for ferry passengers" (≈36 px bold, x≈120–567, y≈75–110) sits over body text at about 19 px regular. It differs from the body in both size and weight, so the eye knows where to start and nothing competes with it.
- **The type scale is lean.** There are only two sizes with a big step between them, so neither looks like a mistake. Keep this when revising rather than adding sizes in between.

(For the director, outside this section: the paragraph lines collide vertically. Leading looks less than the font size, so the lines overlap (y≈140–360). That belongs under Text. The three paragraphs cover separate topics (timetable, bicycles, winter) but have no subheads, so passengers can't jump to the one they need. No line in this section covers that, so it is taste.)

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each element stay clear of the others, with no text or box overlapping or touching another? No.** In all three body paragraphs (x ≈ 120–750, y ≈ 138–360), each line overlaps the lines above and below it. The text looks about 18–19 px tall, but the lines are only about 15 px apart. Descenders run into the ascenders of the next line, for example "forty minutes" (y ≈ 161) into "every" (y ≈ 146), and "on after foot passengers" (y ≈ 240) into "Bicycles ride" (y ≈ 225). The reader can't follow a line across because the eye keeps slipping into the neighbouring one. Each paragraph turns into a grey band that has to be read word by word, and some words, such as "takes about twelve minutes", are partly covered. For a passenger notice that has to be taken in at a glance, this is what stops it working. It looks like a broken line-height setting, possibly a fixed pixel value below the font size, rather than a design choice. The fix is to set the line spacing larger than the text size so no lines collide, about 1.4–1.5× the size for body text. Then make sure the gap between paragraphs stays clearly bigger than the new line spacing. There is no catalog entry for this line, so this is a common-sense judgement: overlapping text is simply unreadable. The Text section's line-spacing question will probably flag the same thing, so the director should merge the two. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- Every edge lines up on one left axis at x ≈ 120: the heading and all three paragraphs share it exactly, with no near-misses. That gives the page a clean, single column to read down.
- The empty space is in one place, an L shape to the right and below the column, not scattered in small gaps. A left-aligned reading column with open space beside it is the usual layout for reading, so the page doesn't look lopsided.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- I couldn't tell whether the overlap appears in every browser and at every width, or only in this capture's rendering. Check the paragraphs' computed `line-height` in a live browser.
- I couldn't zoom in on the overlaps: the crop script was refused, so I worked from the whole image (1280 px wide, readable at full size).

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (each element stays clear of the others, with no text overlapping).

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the space between lines of a paragraph suit its line length, neither cramped nor so loose that the lines drift apart?** No. In all three body paragraphs (x ≈ 120–750, y ≈ 137–360), the lines are about 15 px apart but the type is about 19 px. The line spacing is smaller than the type size, so each line's descenders run into the next line's ascenders: "forty minutes" touches "takes about", "on after foot passengers" touches "the side of the deck", and "crossing leaves the quay" touches "the shelter". The viewer sees a jumble before they see sentences. To read it they have to pick each line out of the overlap, and the eye slips to the wrong line on the way back to the left edge. On a notice that gives times and rules, readers will skip it or misread it. Bringhurst (*Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.2.1) says "Longer measures need more lead than short ones", and Hochuli (*Detail in Typography*, p. 47) says the same. At about 65 characters per line this text needs more than average spacing, and it has less than none. The fix is to set the line height to about 1.4–1.5 times the type size, roughly 27–28 px for 19 px text, and keep the space between paragraphs larger than the space between lines so the three blocks still read as separate. This looks like a CSS line-height set below 1, or a fixed pixel value meant for smaller text. **Defect. Major.**

**What's working.**
- The type plan is simple and right for the job. There is one sans family, with a bold heading at about twice the body size, so the heading clearly leads and nothing competes with it. Keep this when you fix the spacing.
- The line length is about right. Body lines run about 60–70 characters inside Bringhurst's 45–75 range, and the rag is gently uneven with no runts. Once the line spacing is fixed, the paragraphs will read comfortably at this width.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (space between lines)

Walk (color): the image is 1280×800 and fits on one screen, so I worked from the whole image. It's dark gray to near-black text on plain white with no hue anywhere. Small palette: yes. Saturated color kept small: yes, since there is none. Light and dark range: yes, dark text on white holds up in grayscale. Warm and cool: yes, there are no hues to place. Matching colors look the same: yes. No vibrating edges: yes. Status colors: yes, there are none. Color not used alone for meaning: yes. Dark theme: yes, it isn't a dark theme. Every line is yes, so no entries need opening.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The piece uses only near-black text on white, with no accent color. For a plain notice that people read, this gives the strongest possible contrast between text and background. Nothing pulls attention away from reading. Color plays no part in this piece's problems: what goes wrong here, the overlapping lines of body text, belongs to the text section.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks. It is a heading and three paragraphs of text on a white page. The empty right half has no visible frame or broken-image icon, so I can't tell that a picture was meant to go there.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
